The statute §152(c)(2)(A) states that an individual bears a relationship to the taxpayer if such individual is "a child of the taxpayer." Since Bob is Alice's son, Bob qualifies as a child of Alice under section 152(c)(2), making the claim true.

Let me analyze the task carefully.

The question asks: "Alice bears a relationship to Bob under section 152(c)(2)."

The facts state: Alice has a son, Bob, who was born January 31st, 2014.

Looking at section 152(c)(2) of the statute:
"(2) Relationship - For purposes of paragraph (1)(A), an individual bears a relationship to the taxpayer described in this paragraph if such individual is- (A) a child of the taxpayer or a descendant of such a child, or (B) a brother, sister, stepbrother, or stepsister of the taxpayer or a descendant of any such relative."

So the question is whether Alice bears a relationship to Bob under this section.

Wait, I need to re-read this more carefully. Section 152(c)(2) defines when "an individual bears a relationship to the taxpayer." The question asks if "Alice bears a relationship to Bob under section 152(c)(2)."

In the context of the statute, "the taxpayer" would be Alice (the one claiming the exemption), and "an individual" would be Bob (the child). So we're asking: does Bob bear a relationship to Alice under 152(c)(2)?

Since Bob is Alice's son, Bob is "a child of the taxpayer" (Alice). So Bob DOES bear a relationship to Alice under section 152(c)(2)(A).

The question phrasing "Alice bears a relationship to Bob" is a bit odd - technically, the statute defines when a child (the individual) bears a relationship to the taxpayer (Alice). But in common language, this relationship is mutual - if Bob is Alice's child, then Alice is Bob's parent.

I think the answer is Entailment - the claim is true. Bob (the individual) bears a relationship to Alice (the taxpayer) because Bob is Alice's child.
